title: DFS in Reykjavík: Find the path the deep way 🧭
description: Watch DFS explore a street-map graph from start to goal, diving deep along routes before backtracking. This visualization shows how depth-first search builds a traversal tree and handles branching in real-world-like grids.
ig_caption:
🧭✨ **DFS in Reykjavík (Miðborg)**: go deep before you go back! 

In **Depth-First Search (DFS)**, we pick a path and keep going as far as possible, then **backtrack** when we hit dead ends. Graph-theoretically, your city streets become a **graph** (intersections = nodes, streets = edges), and DFS builds a **depth-first spanning tree** (or traversal forest) as it visits vertices.

📍In this visualization, DFS may find a route quickly—or take a longer detour—because DFS prioritizes **depth over shortest distance**. That behavior is exactly what makes DFS powerful for exploring connectivity, detecting cycles, and solving “reachability” style problems.

⚙️ Try it: change the start/end points and watch how the exploration order shifts with the graph’s neighbor ordering. 

👉 **Want the next reel with BFS vs DFS on the same city graph?** Comment “BFS” and follow for more map-based algorithm animations! 🚀
fb_caption:
🚦How does a computer “search” a city map? In this DFS visualization for Reykjavík (Miðborg), we turn streets into a **graph** and intersections into **nodes**, then use **Depth-First Search** to explore deeply along edges until it must backtrack.

🔍 DFS is great for connectivity and traversal—what changes the behavior is the neighbor visitation order and the graph’s branching. Like, share, and comment where you’d like the next city+algorithm comparison!
